facts.statement: Pedeticosaurus was an extinct crocodylomorph that lived in South Africa during the Early Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Pedeticosaurus is an extinct genus of crocodylomorph from the Clarens Formation (Early Jurassic) of South Africa.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is housed in the National Museum in Bloemfontein with the catalog number NMQR606.
facts.quote: It is currently housed in the National Museum in Bloemfontein and cataloged as NMQR606.

facts.statement: The original describer, Van Hoepen, established a new family called Pedeticosauridae for the genus, believing it was closely related to Ornithosuchidae.
facts.quote: Van Hoepen originally established a new family for Pedeticosaurus called Pedeticosauridae, which he thought was closely related to the family Ornithosuchidae.

facts.statement: Later interpretations classified Pedeticosaurus as either a member of Sphenosuchia or Protosuchia, groups of small-bodied Jurassic crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: In later years Pedeticosaurus was interpreted as either a member of Sphenosuchia or Protosuchia, both of which are groups of small-bodied Jurassic crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: In 1968, A. D. Walker erected the group Pedeticosauria, named after the genus, which is now considered equivalent to Sphenosuchia.
facts.quote: Paleontologist A. D. Walker erected a new group called Pedeticosauria in 1968, which he named after Pedeticosaurus and is now considered equivalent to Sphenosuchia.

facts.statement: In 1986, James M. Clark proposed that Pedeticosaurus leviseuri was a synonym of Protosuchus haughtoni based on shared features like a broad scapula and large squamosal bone.
facts.quote: In 1986, James M. Clark proposed that Pedeticosaurus leviseuri was a synonym of the better known protosuchian species Protosuchus haughtoni based on features such as a broad scapula bone with a concave front margin and a large squamosal bone in the skull.

facts.statement: In 2002, Clark and Sues proposed that Pedeticosaurus leviseuri is a nomen dubium because the features of the holotype are too poorly preserved to distinguish it as a valid species.
facts.quote: In 2002, Clark and Hans-Dieter Sues proposed that Pedeticosaurus leviseuri was a nomen dubium or "doubtful name" given that the features in QS 606 are too poorly preserved to distinguish P. leviseuri as its own species.

facts.statement: In 1988, C. E. Gow and James Kitching referred a second skeleton found in the Elliot Formation to the genus Pedeticosaurus.
facts.quote: Paleontologists C. E. Gow and James Kitching of the Bernard Price Institute for Palaeontological Research referred a second skeleton to Pedeticosaurus in 1988.

facts.statement: Gow and Kitching classified the second skeleton as Pedeticosaurus sp. and considered it a sphenosuchian.
facts.quote: Gow and Kitching classified it as Pedeticosaurus sp. and considered it a sphenosuchian.

facts.statement: In 2002, Clark and Sues reassigned the second skeleton (BP/1/5237) to a new genus and species named Litargosuchus leptorhynchus.
facts.quote: In 2002, Clark and Sues assigned BP/1/5237 to a new genus and species of sphenosuchian named Litargosuchus leptorhynchus.

facts.statement: Pedeticosaurus belongs to the parent group Crocodylomorpha.
The time range for Pedeticosaurus is estimated from 199.5 to 192.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Sinemurian to Sinemurian (199.5 to 192.9 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The type species Pedeticosaurus leviseuri was named by Egbert Cornelis Nicolaas van Hoepen in 1915 based on a mold of a mostly complete skeleton found near Rosendal, Free State.
rejected.quote: The type species Pedeticosaurus leviseuri was named by Egbert Cornelis Nicolaas van Hoepen in 1915 on the basis of a mold of a mostly complete skeleton found in a quarry near Rosendal, Free State.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'a mold of a mostly complete skeleton found'

rejected.statement: The fossil mold preserves most of the right half of the skeleton, including the skull, ribs, vertebrae, limbs, tail, and both dermal and ventral osteoderms.
rejected.quote: The mold preserves most of the right half of the skeleton including the skull, ribs, dorsal vertebrae, forelimbs and hindlimbs, tail, and both dermal and ventral osteoderms, separated on two slabs.
